summary:
Yakana's Fire Intelligence is a free web platform that turns 20+ years of NASA satellite fire data into prevention tools for Peru.

NASA's record comes from two sensors, MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m), that count fire differently, so adding them makes fire seem to explode in 2012: a change of camera, not of fire. We harmonized both into one comparable record, with about 13% national monthly error on years the model never saw. On top of it, a logistic-regression model estimates the chance of fire per 6.6 km zone. Tested on 2019-2025 using only earlier years, it reaches AUC 0.89, and 84% of the zones it flags did burn. We compared five methods and kept the logistic model because it gives readable probabilities.

Families check their home against nearby fires and an 8-week and 14-day forecast, then alert relatives in one tap. Firefighters get a response view with coordinates and printable reports. An explorer shows a 23-year fire calendar on real 3D terrain, and YakaLlama, our bilingual assistant, answers questions. Data refreshes automatically from NASA FIRMS.

Fires threaten lives, farms and forest in Peru, and prevention only works when trustworthy data reaches everyone, not just scientists.
details:
YAKANA'S FIRE INTELLIGENCE

How it works:

A Python pipeline downloads NASA FIRMS hotspots (MODIS, VIIRS), keeps vegetation fires of nominal/high confidence and one VIIRS satellite per day, and fits a per-department log-log model on the 2012-2022 overlap to convert MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent counts, with an uncertainty range. A second pipeline builds 11 features per 6.6 km zone from earlier years only and trains a logistic regression, chosen after comparing five methods.

Benefits and impact:

Scientists get an honest 23-year series. Families check their home and share alerts. Firefighters get coordinates and printable reports. The aim: earlier action, fewer losses.

Tools:

  • Data: NASA FIRMS and GIBS, AWS Terrain Tiles, Sentinel-2 cloudless, OpenStreetMap.
  • Backend: Python, pandas, scikit-learn, FastAPI, DuckDB, Docker, on Google Cloud Run + Cloud Storage (NASA-provided credits).
  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Next.js, Tailwind, three.js, on Vercel.
  • Automation: GitHub Actions (daily refresh), Google Cloud Run Jobs.
  • AI: NVIDIA-hosted LLM (YakaLlama).

Creativity:

A lens compares real MODIS and VIIRS pixels, fire clocks show a typical year for Coast, Highlands and Rainforest, and real hotspots rise on 3D terrain. YakaLlama, a bilingual assistant, answers from our own data.

What we considered:

  • Honesty: validation on unseen years, uncertainty ranges, no weather data (stated openly).
  • Privacy: saved places are stored only on your device
  • Safety: not an emergency service; points to "Bomberos" 116.
  • Access: free, no account, EN/ES, data snapshot if the API fails.

AI use disclosure:

  • Building AI/ML into the project: YakaLlama, the in-app assistant, uses an NVIDIA-hosted language model. It answers only from the site's content and our backend data and cites its source. The fire-risk forecast uses a logistic regression we trained and validated ourselves; it is statistics, not a generative model.
  • Coding, debugging and troubleshooting: AI coding assistants (Claude Code and Cursor) helped write, review and debug code and draft documentation (README). The team set the goals, made the design and data decisions, ran the code and verified the results.
  • Images, video and audio: The audio and edit of the video pitch were generated with AI tools. Everything else in the video was made by the team.
  • NASA branding: no AI-generated content uses or modifies NASA logos or identifiers. The NASA logo appears unmodified only to name the challenge.
  • Data: all fire data are real NASA FIRMS records; no data were generated by AI.
GitHub repository: https://github.com/SebasHuaypar/Yakanas-NASA
